title: SFA: A Statistical Physics-Inspired Diffusion Transformer for Efficient and High-Quality Image Generation

paper.title:
SFA: A Statistical Physics-Inspired
Diffusion Transformer for Efficient
and High-Quality Image Generation
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion transformers have achieved remarkable success in image generation, but accelerating attention while preserving generation quality remains a major challenge at high resolutions. Inspired by statistical physics and the widespread occurrence of scale-free laws in nature, we introduce Scale-Free Attention (SFA), which preserves fine local interactions while summarizing distant regions at progressively coarser scales. For N N tokens, mean pooling, token-count correction, and a shared softmax over a scale-free spatial hierarchy give SFA O ⁡ ( N ​ log ⁡ N ) O(N\log N) complexity in both forward and backward passes. Our Triton implementation achieves 357.3 × 357.3\times forward and 265.6 × 265.6\times backward attention speedups over FlashAttention at 262,144 tokens. After 40 epochs of PixelFlow training from scratch on ImageNet at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution, SFA achieves the best generation quality among five attention mechanisms, including full attention. Fréchet inception distance evaluated on 50,000 generated samples (FID-50k) improves from 13.25 for full attention to 12.51, and the advantage over full attention persists through 80 epochs. SFA also achieves the best generation quality among the compared efficient-attention methods on Flickr-Faces-HQ (FFHQ). Beyond training from scratch, Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium with attention replaced by SFA retains the generation quality of its full-attention counterpart under matched fine-tuning budgets. We obtain similar results when fine-tuning pretrained PixelFlow on ImageNet. SFA establishes scale-free structure as an effective design principle for efficient, high-quality diffusion transformers.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Generating coherent visual content at high resolution requires models that capture both fine detail and long-range structure. Diffusion transformers (DiTs) have achieved strong image-generation performance by combining scalable transformer backbones with iterative denoising ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) . However, the quadratic cost of all-to-all attention becomes a major constraint as spatial resolution grows, particularly for direct pixel-space generation with PixelFlow ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . Substantially reducing this cost while matching or exceeding the generation quality of full attention remains an open problem. Existing approaches address different parts of this challenge. FlashAttention improves exact attention through memory-efficient tiling and parallel execution ( Dao et al., 2022 ; Dao, 2024 ) . Its arithmetic cost remains quadratic in token count. Linear attention uses feature-map aggregation to reduce this cost to linear complexity ( Katharopoulos et al., 2020 ; Choromanski et al., 2021 ) . However, the finite feature representations underlying this efficiency trade computational cost against approximation fidelity, making preservation of pretrained softmax interactions a separate challenge. Sparse methods such as Log-linear Sparse Attention (LLSA) ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) reduce interactions through hierarchical selection. Selection adds runtime overhead and omits fine interactions outside the selected regions, which can limit generation quality. Hierarchical attention offers structured global approximations, with H-Transformer-1D ( Zhu & Soricut, 2021 ) developed for one-dimensional sequences. Fast Multipole Attention (FMA) ( Kang et al., 2025 ) extends multilevel computation to image classification tasks using learned pooling and separate softmax at each scale, which complicates efficient kernel implementation and precludes direct resolution extrapolation and drop-in fine-tuning from full-attention checkpoints. These limitations restrict its applicability to long sequences and large pretrained generative models. The remaining challenge is to combine subquadratic cost, efficient execution, and generation quality competitive with full attention in both training from scratch and adaptation. Scale-free laws, widely studied in statistical physics, appear in natural images as approximate scale invariance and power spectra close to an inverse-square law ( Field, 1987 ; Ruderman & Bialek, 1994 ) . Consistent with this spatial prior, we observe an approximate power law in the aggregate radial attention of pretrained PixelFlow, whereas random initialization gives a nearly flat profile (Figure 1 (C)). Motivated by this observation, we introduce Scale-Free Attention (SFA) , which preserves exact local interactions and partitions the remaining image into progressively larger blocks, each represented by its mean key and value. SFA adds the logarithm of each block’s token count to its logit and applies a single softmax to all local tokens and block summaries. Our contributions are threefold.

sections.heading: Scale-free attention.
sections.text: By combining mean pooling, a log ⁡ | B | \log|B| correction for spatial blocks B B containing | B | |B| tokens, and a shared softmax over a two-dimensional scale-free hierarchy, SFA retains the original attention projections without additional parameters or hyperparameters. For N N tokens, both forward and backward passes have O ⁡ ( N ​ log ⁡ N ) O(N\log N) complexity. In our experiments, SFA achieves higher generation quality than the three efficient-attention baselines and matches or exceeds the performance of full attention (Figure 2 (C,D)).

sections.heading: Fast Triton kernels.
sections.text: We implement SFA in Triton ( Tillet et al., 2019 ) , using recursive pooling and kernels that fuse attention across spatial scales. Figures 4 and 5 in Appendix B illustrate the forward and backward kernel architectures, respectively. At 262,144 tokens, SFA achieves 357.3 × 357.3\times forward and 265.6 × 265.6\times backward speedups over FlashAttention on an RTX 5090 (Figure 2 (A,B)).

sections.heading: Approximation guarantees.
sections.text: For a fixed spatial partition, we prove that SFA uniquely minimizes reverse Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence to full attention among blockwise uniform distributions, and bound attention-mass and output errors under logarithmic spatial logits.

sections.heading: Generative modeling.
sections.text: Denoising diffusion models learn to reverse gradual corruption ( Ho et al., 2020 ) , while score-based models describe generation through reverse-time stochastic dynamics ( Song et al., 2021 ) . Flow matching learns vector fields along prescribed probability paths ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) , and rectified flow uses straight interpolations between noise and data ( Liu et al., 2023 ) . These objectives can operate in different representations: latent diffusion reduces spatial computation through learned compression ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , whereas PixelFlow generates directly in pixel space through a resolution cascade ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . Diffusion transformers apply scalable transformer backbones to latent patches ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ; Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) , improving generation as model capacity and token count increase, and multimodal rectified flow transformers extend attention to joint image–text interactions ( Esser et al., 2024 ) . sections.heading: Efficient diffusion attention.
sections.text: Trainable efficient attention reduces interaction cost while allowing the generator to adapt to the resulting operator. For pretrained generators, compatibility with existing projections and output resolution further supports adaptation through fine-tuning. Recent approaches differ in how they allocate computation: Combiner ( Ren et al., 2021 ) extends sparse attention patterns with indirect attention to regional summaries, providing a global receptive field. FMMformer ( Nguyen et al., 2021 ) computes near- and far-field interactions separately, using an approach similar to linear attention for the latter. Hourglass Diffusion Transformer (HDiT) ( Crowson et al., 2024 ) uses low-resolution global self-attention for coherence. Piecewise Sparse Attention (PISA) ( Li et al., 2026 ) uses dynamic block selection and Taylor approximation of weakly correlated blocks. Video Sparse Attention (VSA) ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) selects important blocks using pooled features, and Sparse-Linear Attention (SLA) ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) combines sparse interactions with a linear component. Log-linear Sparse Attention (LLSA) ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) performs hierarchical selection, enriching fine tokens with pooled keys and values from multiple scales. SFA likewise uses recursive means and shared attention computation. Its fixed spatial interaction lists maintain global coverage through a content-independent allocation of resolution. Appendix D.1 further compares SFA with Sana ( Xie et al., 2025 ) and Native Sparse Attention (NSA) ( Yuan et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Multiscale approximation.
sections.text: This fixed spatial construction connects SFA to multiscale attention approximations. FMA ( Kang et al., 2025 ) uses learned pooling kernels and separate softmax at each scale. H-Transformer-1D ( Zhu & Soricut, 2021 ) operates on one-dimensional sequences and also coarse-grains queries. Multi Resolution Analysis (MRA) ( Zeng et al., 2022 ) coarsens queries and uses data-driven criteria to determine where coarsening is appropriate. Focal Attention ( Yang et al., 2021 ) uses multiscale overlapping partitions and introduces learnable pooling, whereas Radial Attention ( Li et al., 2025 ) reduces interactions with spatiotemporally distant video patches. Token Merging ( Bolya et al., 2023 ) combines similar tokens in vision transformers, reducing the sequence length passed to subsequent layers and adding a log token-count bias to the attention logits. Further comparisons appear in Appendix D .

sections.heading: 3.1 Spatial scale as a guide to attention
sections.text: To choose the spatial resolution of attention, we use the scale structure of natural images illustrated in Figure 1 (A,B). An isotropic finite-band approximation to their inverse-square power spectra ( Ruderman & Bialek, 1994 ) gives logarithmic spatial correlation over intermediate distances in two dimensions (Appendix A.1 ). Define the distance between distinct tokens as r i ​ j = ‖ 𝒙 i − 𝒙 j ‖ 2 > 0 r_{ij}=\|{\bm{x}}_{i}-{\bm{x}}_{j}\|_{2}>0 and fix a reference distance r ∗ > 0 r_{*}>0 . If query–key interactions inherit this dependence, their logits admit a radial model with query-dependent offset b i b_{i} , decay exponent α i ≥ 0 \alpha_{i}\geq 0 , and content residual u i ​ j u_{ij} : z i ​ j = b i − α i ​ log ⁡ ( r i ​ j / r ∗ ) + u i ​ j , α i ≥ 0 . z_{ij}=b_{i}-\alpha_{i}\log(r_{ij}/r_{*})+u_{ij},\qquad\alpha_{i}\geq 0. (2) The radial weights exp ⁡ ( z i ​ j − u i ​ j ) ∝ r i ​ j − α i \exp(z_{ij}-u_{ij})\propto r_{ij}^{-\alpha_{i}} vary by the same factor over any fixed distance ratio. Section 5.2 and Appendix C.7 present the corresponding empirical measurements. This power law motivates the growth of block sizes in proportion to distance. The pretrained attention profile in Figure 1 (C) supports this spatial allocation, within which content-dependent dot products allow the model to learn interaction strengths.

sections.heading: 3.2 A complete multiscale partition
sections.text: SFA realizes this allocation through a scale-free two-dimensional hierarchical partition similar to that in FMA ( Kang et al., 2025 ) and H-Transformer ( Zhu & Soricut, 2021 ) . Each query belongs to a 4 × 4 4\times 4 base block whose 3 × 3 3\times 3 block neighborhood, clipped to the image boundary, supplies at most 144 exact singleton tokens. Distant regions are represented through a quadtree. At each pooled scale, we take the children of the 3 × 3 3\times 3 neighborhood around the query ancestor’s parent and exclude the ancestor’s own 3 × 3 3\times 3 neighborhood. This leaves at most 27 blocks per scale, with side lengths doubling at successive scales. This construction covers the entire image. Together with the exact local tokens, the pooled blocks form a complete, disjoint partition 𝒫 i \mathcal{P}_{i} for query i i : every original token belongs to exactly one represented block. The 16 queries in each base block share this partition while retaining their original resolution and computing their own attention weights. Figure 1 (D) illustrates this coverage; Appendix B.1 specifies the interaction lists and boundary handling.

A shared softmax jointly normalizes their count-corrected logits across all scales. Related token-count corrections appear in token merging ( Bolya et al., 2023 ) .

sections.heading: 3.4 Linear preprocessing and log-linear attention
sections.text: After pooling base blocks, each coarser mean averages four child means, allowing summaries to be constructed once and shared across queries. The geometric decrease in summary counts gives O ⁡ ( N ⁡ ( d + d v ) ) O(N(d+d_{v})) preprocessing, while constant representatives per scale give O ⁡ ( N ⁡ ( d + d v ) ​ log ⁡ N ) O(N(d+d_{v})\log N) forward and backward cost. Our Triton kernels reuse shared data and fuse attention across scales, with forward and backward architectures detailed in Appendix B (Figures 4 and 5 ). SFA retains the original projections, head dimensions, and output shape, enabling direct reuse of pretrained weights.

sections.heading: A preference for coherent far-field signals.
sections.text: The same aggregation also shapes the information available during training. At fixed block masses and with weights independent of the value noise, uniform aggregation minimizes output noise variance under independent, equal-variance noise. This favors coherent far-field signals while exact local interactions retain fine detail (Appendix A.8 ). Pooling after RoPE further acts as a low-pass filter on position-modulated keys, with bandwidth decreasing as block size grows (Appendix A.9 ). These properties give SFA a spatial inductive bias for image generation alongside its controlled approximation of pretrained attention.

sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental setup
sections.text: Our baselines are LLSA ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) , SLA ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and VSA ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , using their official Triton implementations and matching the selected-block budgets of SLA and VSA to LLSA. Full attention provides an additional reference for ImageNet generation and efficiency measurements. Figure 2 (E) shows representative generated images. We evaluate PixelFlow ( Chen et al., 2025 ) on ImageNet at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution ( Deng et al., 2009 ) , replacing attention in its highest-resolution stage of 4096 tokens and retaining full attention in the other three stages. For longer spatial sequences, we use the small DiT variant (DiT-S; Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) in pixel space on FFHQ ( Karras et al., 2019 ) at resolutions 128, 256, and 512, following the resolution cascade of LLSA in which each resolution continues from the preceding one (Table 3 ). FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) and inception score (IS; Salimans et al., 2016 ) use 50,000 generated samples, and all throughput measurements use one NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. Appendix C gives the detailed configurations, evaluation protocols, and fixed-rate baseline comparisons.

sections.heading: 5.2 Spatial statistics of pretrained attention
sections.text: In pretrained PixelFlow-XL, geometric-mean radial attention s geo ​ ( r ) s_{\mathrm{geo}}(r) at distance r r follows s geo ​ ( r ) ∝ r − α s_{\mathrm{geo}}(r)\propto r^{-\alpha} with α = 1.414 \alpha=1.414 over 8–160 pixels (Figure 1 (C)). The power-law fit achieves R 2 = 0.974 R^{2}=0.974 , compared with 0.589 for logarithmic decay, both evaluated on the original attention scale. By contrast, random initialization produces a nearly uniform radial profile, indicating that the spatial scaling emerges through training and supporting SFA’s prior. sections.heading: 5.3 Attention and end-to-end efficiency
sections.text: Compared with FlashAttention, SFA’s forward and backward speedups increase from 2.99 × 2.99\times and 2.50 × 2.50\times at 4096 tokens to 357.3 × 357.3\times and 265.6 × 265.6\times at 262,144 tokens (Figure 2 (A,B)). At the largest scale, SFA’s forward and backward speedups over LLSA are 4.70 × 4.70\times and 4.45 × 4.45\times , respectively. End-to-end gains are bounded by projections, feed-forward networks, and other computations outside attention. The kernel gains above yield 25.75 × 25.75\times faster training and 22.54 × 22.54\times faster generation on FFHQ at 512 × 512 512\times 512 resolution, relative to full attention. In Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium at 2048 × 2048 2048\times 2048 , replacing both image self-attention and image-to-image interactions in joint attention (preserving all other interactions) gives 2.10 × 2.10\times training and 1.97 × 1.97\times generation speedups over full attention. It should be emphasized that on FFHQ, SFA achieves nearly constant token throughput at a fixed training token batch, demonstrating that attention is no longer the computational bottleneck even at 262,144 tokens per sequence. Tables 4 , 5 , 7 , and 12 provide the full kernel, FFHQ, PixelFlow, and Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium measurements, respectively. Across these model-level comparisons, SFA’s memory consumption remains close to the FlashAttention baseline.

sections.heading: 5.5 Adapting pretrained generators
sections.text: We fine-tune the original PixelFlow model and a model with SFA in its highest-resolution stage from the same checkpoint under an identical schedule. After 3.5 epochs, full attention reaches FID 50k of 2.28 and IS of 273.25, compared with 2.29 and 284.71 for SFA, using the same 50,000-sample evaluation protocol (Table 11 ). SFA thus retains comparable FID and improves IS under the matched budget, preserving generation quality with the original projections and parameter count. For Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium ( Stability AI, 2024 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) , we retain the original effective patch size of 16 × 16 16\times 16 pixels and replace image self-attention alone (SA), which the first 13 of its 24 blocks carry, or together with image-to-image interactions in the joint attention of all 24 blocks (ALL). After one epoch of matched fine-tuning, both scopes recover the quality of the equally fine-tuned original model. ALL achieves a Dense Prompt Graph Benchmark (DPG-Bench; Hu et al., 2024 ) score of 85.51, matching full attention, and a human preference score (HPS) v2.1 ( Wu et al., 2023 ) of 30.262, compared with 30.261 for full attention. The joint-attention replacement is specified in Appendix C.6 , with the complete direct-replacement and fine-tuning comparisons in Tables 13 – 15 .

sections.heading: 5.6 Ablations
sections.text: We evaluate four variants to examine count correction, normalization across scales, far-field context, and aggregation. Under the FFHQ- 128 128 setup above, removing the log ⁡ m B \log m_{B} correction raises FID 50k from 22.91 to 25.91, and normalizing each scale separately, as FMA does, raises it to 27.99. Retaining only the exact 12 × 12 12\times 12 local neighborhood raises it to 45.76, supporting the contribution of far-field summaries. The first two changes also reduce quality under direct image self-attention replacement in Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium without fine-tuning. In particular, separate softmax lowers overall HPS v2.1 from 29.596 for SFA to 11.176 and produces grid-like artifacts. On ImageNet- 256 256 , replacing mean pooling with learnable aggregation and removing count correction raises FID 50k from 40.66 to 41.40 and lowers IS from 32.90 to 31.50 after ten epochs. In our RTX 5090 implementation, this variant also takes 1.96 1.96 – 2.64 × 2.64\times SFA’s forward attention time and 2.89 2.89 – 4.74 × 4.74\times its backward attention time across the tested sequence lengths of 4096–262,144 tokens. These results support the combination of mean pooling, count correction, and shared normalization. Appendix C.8 gives the four variant definitions, detailed quality results, and efficiency analysis.

sections.heading: 6 Discussion and Limitations
sections.text: The spatial hierarchy in SFA suggests a natural extension to video generation through spatiotemporal partitioning. Such a hierarchy could preserve fine interactions within nearby frames while summarizing increasingly distant regions across both space and time. Mean pooling, token-count correction, and shared normalization apply to these spatiotemporal blocks, with motion and the different rates of spatial and temporal variation guiding their shapes and resolutions. Adapting temporal coarsening to these correlations throughout denoising would be a promising direction for balancing generation quality and computational cost. Beyond video generation, this principle could support action-conditioned visual world models, which predict how an environment evolves in response to actions ( Bruce et al., 2024 ) . A hierarchy over past observations could retain detailed interactions with recent frames and conditioning actions while representing older visual context through coarser summaries, potentially making longer histories more affordable during prediction. In a causal formulation, each pooled summary and its token count would need to include only the history visible to its query. The resulting partition would thus need to respect both spatiotemporal structure and causal ordering. Our study focuses on regular two-dimensional image grids, leaving irregular grids unexplored. Additionally, further acceleration is constrained by the remaining transformer components: our FFHQ experiments show that the computational bottleneck has shifted from attention to projections, feed-forward networks, and other operations. Optimizing the transformer block as a whole therefore remains a direction for future work.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: By combining a scale-free spatial partition with mean aggregation, token-count correction, and a single softmax across scales, SFA gives an O ⁡ ( N ​ log ⁡ N ) O(N\log N) attention mechanism with a precise approximation relationship to full attention and a spatial inductive bias suited to image generation. Our analysis links approximation quality to within-block logit variation and explains why relative spatial resolution is appropriate for power-law interactions. Empirically, SFA achieves the best quality in the five-method PixelFlow comparison at 40 epochs, improves FFHQ generation, and preserves full-attention quality under matched fine-tuning budgets in PixelFlow and Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium. Together with substantial attention and whole-model speedups, these results support its use in both training new generators and adapting pretrained ones.

Our experiments use existing public image datasets, including FFHQ, which contains photographs of real people. We acknowledge the privacy concerns and demographic biases associated with such datasets, and the importance of respecting their licenses and usage restrictions. No real images from the FFHQ dataset are displayed in this manuscript. sections.heading: Organization of the analysis.
sections.text: We develop the approximation results by following how pooling changes an attention distribution. Appendix A.1 first connects inverse-square image spectra to the logarithmic spatial model. Appendix A.2 then proves SFA’s reverse-KL optimality for arbitrary finite logits. The quantitative error analysis proceeds through two probability inequalities (Appendix A.3 ), an exact separation of block-mass and within-block errors (Appendix A.4 ), and the scale-consistent bounds of Theorem 4.2 (Appendix A.5 ). Appendix A.6 expresses the same error through query-projected feature statistics. Appendices A.7 – A.10 then explain the associated spatial bias: mass across distance shells, noise reduction by averaging, the frequency response after rotary encoding, and the special geometry of the two-dimensional logarithmic model.

sections.heading: Appendix B Details of the Triton Kernel Implementation
sections.text: This section follows the computation of SFA and its gradients. After introducing the notation in Appendix B.1 , we describe the forward pass in Appendix B.2 : constructing block means, sharing their loads across queries, and accumulating one softmax across scales. Appendix B.3 follows the backward pass from probability recomputation to the final query, key, and value gradients. At each step, we explain how the hierarchy enables data reuse and reduces memory traffic. The exact and finest pooled windows are generated from coordinates; coarser lists are read from the cached indices. These masks preserve each query’s partition while avoiding a separately gathered candidate tensor for every query.

sections.heading: Compute query gradients (B1).
sections.text: One program owns the 16 queries of a base block. It computes and saves D i D_{i} , revisits the exact and pooled candidates, and accumulates each query gradient in float32 before storing it. Each query has a unique writer, while the saved D i D_{i} values are reused by both key and value gradient computations.

sections.heading: Combine gradients of shared summaries (B3).
sections.text: Several query programs can update the same pooled representative. Each program first combines the contributions of a group of query blocks. At ℓ = 0 \ell=0 , one program processes four sibling query blocks against a shared set of at most 36 candidates, retaining the per-query exclusion masks. At ℓ ≥ 1 \ell\geq 1 , identical interaction lists allow one program to combine c ℓ = min ⁡ ( 4 ℓ , 32 ) c_{\ell}=\min(4^{\ell},32) base query blocks. It loads the pooled keys and values once, processes 32 query rows at a time, and accumulates their contributions in registers. Atomic additions then write the combined gradients to initially zero float32 buffers. Relative to separate base-block programs, grouping reduces shared-candidate loads and gradient updates by a factor of c ℓ c_{\ell} at these coarser levels.

sections.heading: Propagate through the means (T4).
sections.text: All 16 tokens in a base block receive the same gradient share from every pooled ancestor. Let g ∈ { 0 , … , G − 1 } g\in\{0,\ldots,G-1\} be its Morton index, and let 𝒅 ℓ , t K , 𝒅 ℓ , t V {\bm{d}}_{\ell,t}^{K},{\bm{d}}_{\ell,t}^{V} denote the direct gradients of level- ℓ \ell block t t . Its ancestor index is ⌊ g / 4 ℓ ⌋ \lfloor g/4^{\ell}\rfloor , so the per-token pooled contributions are 𝒔 g K \displaystyle{\bm{s}}_{g}^{K} = ∑ ℓ = 0 n lev − 1 𝒅 ℓ , ⌊ g / 4 ℓ ⌋ K 16 ⋅ 4 ℓ , \displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=0}^{n_{\mathrm{lev}}-1}\frac{{\bm{d}}_{\ell,\lfloor g/4^{\ell}\rfloor}^{K}}{16\cdot 4^{\ell}}, (52) 𝒔 g V \displaystyle{\bm{s}}_{g}^{V} = ∑ ℓ = 0 n lev − 1 𝒅 ℓ , ⌊ g / 4 ℓ ⌋ V 16 ⋅ 4 ℓ . \displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=0}^{n_{\mathrm{lev}}-1}\frac{{\bm{d}}_{\ell,\lfloor g/4^{\ell}\rfloor}^{V}}{16\cdot 4^{\ell}}. (53) The denominator is the number of original tokens in the corresponding mean. A single kernel sums these ancestor contributions for both keys and values, accumulating in float32 and storing one vector per base block in the input format. This completes the chain rule through the hierarchy in compact arrays of shape [ n b , n h , G , d ] [n_{b},n_{h},G,d] .

sections.heading: Write the original key and value gradients (B2).
sections.text: Finally, one program owns the 16 original keys and values in each base block. Symmetry of the exact neighborhood identifies all queries that attend to those tokens directly. The program accumulates these exact contributions, adds 𝒔 g K {\bm{s}}_{g}^{K} and 𝒔 g V {\bm{s}}_{g}^{V} to each token’s corresponding gradients, and performs the final stores. Thus the full-resolution gradients have unique writers, and the pooled contribution needs neither a full-resolution intermediate buffer nor a separate addition pass. The saved mean hierarchy, pooled-gradient buffers, and base-block shares all contain O ⁡ ( n b ​ n h ​ N ​ d ) O(n_{b}n_{h}Nd) floating-point entries. Integer geometry is cached separately and shared across batches and heads.

SLA uses query and key/value blocks of 64 tokens and the softmax feature map in its linear branch, and VSA uses block shape ( 1 , 8 , 8 ) (1,8,8) , whose unit temporal dimension corresponds to image inputs. Accounting for these different block sizes, the budget-matched SLA and VSA kernel settings select 4, 5, 8, and 20 key/value blocks for spatial grid sides L = 64,128,256,512 L=64,128,256,512 , respectively, matching LLSA up to block rounding. At L = 64 L=64 , we round the selected-block budget down to four blocks in the isolated kernel benchmark and up to five blocks in generation-quality experiments. The higher sparsity in the kernel benchmark favors SLA and VSA’s throughput, and the denser attention in generation experiments favors their quality, making both comparisons more demanding for SFA. Model-level throughput uses the same five-block configuration as generation quality. sections.heading: C.6 Fine-tuning Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium
sections.text: We extend the evaluation to pretrained text-to-image generation with Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium ( Stability AI, 2024 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) , retaining its original image tokenization. Its variational autoencoder (VAE) compresses each spatial dimension by a factor of 8, after which the transformer embeds 2 × 2 2\times 2 latent patches, producing an effective patch size of 16 × 16 16\times 16 pixels. Image resolutions of 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 and 2048 × 2048 2048\times 2048 consequently give 64 × 64 64\times 64 and 128 × 128 128\times 128 image-token grids with 4096 and 16,384 image tokens, respectively. Joint attention combines these image tokens with the text tokens. To distinguish the effect of attention replacement from subsequent adaptation, we compare six attention and fine-tuning settings. Of the 24 transformer blocks, the first 13 contain a separate image self-attention module alongside the joint attention. Full retains the original attention, and the self-attention-only setting (SA) replaces those 13 modules with SFA. ALL extends the replacement to the image-to-image interactions inside the joint attention of all 24 blocks, preserving the original computation for text-to-text, text-to-image, and image-to-text interactions. Image and text contributions share one softmax normalizer for each query. Because ALL covers more of the quadratic attention work, it reaches a larger speedup than SA at both resolutions (Table 12 ). The suffix +ft identifies a fine-tuned checkpoint. The quality tables group Full, SA, and ALL together, followed by Full+ft, SA+ft, and ALL+ft, so that each group compares methods within a shared adaptation budget.

Training uses AdamW with weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} , gradient-norm clipping 1.0, bfloat16 parameters and optimizer states, and gradient checkpointing. All models start from the same pretrained checkpoint, and we evaluate their raw checkpoint weights.

sections.heading: C.8 Ablations
sections.text: We examine count correction, normalization across scales, far-field context, and block aggregation through four variants of SFA. We first report their generation quality and then analyze how these design choices affect computational efficiency. Variant 1 removes the log ⁡ | B | \log|B| correction while retaining mean pooling and shared softmax. Variant 2 retains mean pooling but applies softmax separately at each scale and sums the resulting outputs. Variant 3 retains only SFA’s exact local neighborhood: the 3 × 3 3\times 3 neighborhood of 4 × 4 4\times 4 base blocks, covering 12 × 12 12\times 12 tokens away from image boundaries. It applies softmax over these local tokens and omits all pooled far-field representatives, with the neighborhood clipped at image boundaries. Variant 4 replaces mean pooling with learnable aggregation and omits the log ⁡ | B | \log|B| correction, as FMA does ( Kang et al., 2025 ) , while retaining shared softmax.

sections.heading: Interpretation.
sections.text: Variant 1 supports weighting pooled blocks by their original token counts, and Variant 2 shows the benefit of normalizing all scales together. Their Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium results also connect these choices to pretrained-weight reuse. Variant 3 demonstrates that pooled far-field information improves generation beyond the exact local branch. Finally, the comparison with Variant 4 favors SFA’s mean pooling with count correction over learnable aggregation without that correction at the same ten-epoch budget.

sections.heading: Efficiency.
sections.text: Variants 1 and 3 run at approximately the same speed as SFA in our experiments, despite substantially lower generation quality. Variant 2 introduces a separate softmax denominator and output-dependent gradient correction at every scale. Each query therefore requires scale-specific normalization and backward statistics, giving up the shared normalization and gradient correction used by SFA across all interactions. Variant 4 loses two useful properties of mean pooling. Independently learned aggregation weights at different scales generally prevent a parent representative from being constructed from its four existing child summaries, removing the inexpensive recursive construction available to SFA. During backward, spatially varying weights require distinct gradient contributions for individual token positions, replacing SFA’s uniform gradient sharing within each base block; learning those weights adds parameter-gradient computations. These structural differences increase aggregation and differentiation work and remove the computational reuse described in Appendix B . Our current implementation of Variant 4 shows a substantial runtime penalty on an RTX 5090 with batch size 4, six heads, head dimension 64, and bfloat16 inputs. For N = 4096 , 16384 , 65536 , 262144 N=4096,16384,65536,262144 tokens, its forward runtimes are 2.64 × 2.64\times , 2.27 × 2.27\times , 1.96 × 1.96\times , and 1.98 × 1.98\times those of SFA; its backward runtimes are 4.74 × 4.74\times , 2.89 × 2.89\times , 3.10 × 3.10\times , and 3.14 × 3.14\times , respectively. This slowdown substantially reduces or even eliminates the speed advantage over other efficient-attention mechanisms. Timings are medians after warmup. Forward is measured without gradient recording and includes aggregation; backward is measured separately on a retained graph and includes gradients through aggregation and its learned weights.

sections.heading: Appendix D Extended Related Work
sections.text: The attention comparisons in Section 2 draw on broader work in computational efficiency, spatial hierarchies, and image statistics.

sections.heading: D.1 Linear and hardware-efficient attention
sections.text: Attention efficiency depends on both the representation of interactions and their implementation. FlashAttention ( Dao et al., 2022 ) reduces memory traffic through tiled exact attention, and FlashAttention-2 ( Dao, 2024 ) improves work partitioning and parallelism. However, their dense arithmetic remains quadratic in token count. Linear attention addresses this arithmetic cost through kernel feature maps and associative multiplication ( Katharopoulos et al., 2020 ) , with Performer approximating the softmax kernel through positive random features ( Choromanski et al., 2021 ) . Kernel approximations and memory-efficient implementations therefore address distinct components of attention cost. SFA combines an O ⁡ ( N ​ log ⁡ N ) O(N\log N) attention architecture that delivers strong generative performance with a computationally efficient Triton implementation. In diffusion models, Sana demonstrates the use of linear attention in a high-resolution diffusion architecture ( Xie et al., 2025 ) . Native Sparse Attention (NSA) combines compressed representations, selected blocks, and a local window in language models ( Yuan et al., 2025 ) . These approaches allocate computation through a kernel representation or several attention branches; SFA instead assigns spatial resolution through a complete, query-specific partition of the token grid.

sections.heading: D.2 Spatial hierarchies
sections.text: Spatial hierarchies provide a structured allocation of computation by representing interactions at different resolutions. For example, Swin Transformer ( Liu et al., 2021 ) uses shifted local windows, and H-Transformer-1D ( Zhu & Soricut, 2021 ) constructs a one-dimensional hierarchical matrix approximation. For long-range interactions, Focal attention ( Yang et al., 2021 ) combines fine local tokens and coarse distant learnable summaries in one softmax, retaining overlapping representations of regions across scales. QuadTree attention ( Tang et al., 2022 ) instead makes refinement content dependent, building pooled query and key pyramids and selecting relevant coarse regions before evaluating finer interactions. This content-dependent refinement contrasts with SFA’s fixed distance-dependent allocation, and the methods also differ in how they aggregate contributions across levels. The methods mentioned above and in Section 2 all differ from SFA. SFA introduces no additional parameters and supports both effective reuse of pretrained weights and high-quality generation when trained from scratch. Our comparison with LLSA shows that SFA’s fixed spatial hierarchy achieves higher kernel throughput and better generation quality than hierarchical dynamic selection. The four ablations in Section 5.6 and Appendix C.8 further demonstrate the necessity of various components of our approach. Variants 1 and 2 remove count correction and normalize scales separately, respectively; both reduce quality in FFHQ- 128 128 training and in direct self-attention replacement for Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium without fine-tuning. Variant 3 retains only the exact local neighborhood, causing a substantial loss of FFHQ generation quality and demonstrating the contribution of pooled far-field context. Variant 4 replaces mean pooling with learnable aggregation and removes count correction, yielding worse FID and IS than SFA under the same ten-epoch PixelFlow training budget. Together, these comparisons support the combination of global coverage, mean pooling, count correction, and shared normalization. These choices also support the kernel efficiencies detailed in Appendix B . Shared softmax reuses normalization and gradient statistics across scales, while mean pooling enables recursive preprocessing and uniform gradient propagation within each base block. Variants 2 and 4 lose these respective forms of computational reuse, with their efficiency consequences analyzed in Appendix C.8 . In the FFHQ measurements, SFA reduces attention’s share of runtime sufficiently for other transformer components to dominate, yielding nearly constant token throughput at a fixed token batch across resolutions. Further end-to-end acceleration therefore depends on optimizing those components.

sections.heading: D.3 Natural-image statistics and positional frequencies
sections.text: The spatial prior underlying SFA has roots in classical studies that connect natural-image statistics to efficient spatial representations ( Field, 1987 ; Simoncelli & Olshausen, 2001 ) and document approximate scale invariance ( Ruderman & Bialek, 1994 ) . In two dimensions, an inverse-square spectrum distributes comparable energy across spatial octaves, motivating attention resolution relative to distance. A related connection between frequency and image structure appears in diffusion models, where Kadkhodaie et al. (2024) relate generalization to denoising in harmonic bases adapted to image geometry. Within attention, positional encoding adds another source of frequency dependence by determining how spatial phase enters the computation. Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) express relative positions through rotations ( Su et al., 2024 ) and have effective two-dimensional constructions for vision transformers ( Heo et al., 2024 ) . Studies of trained language models further reveal distinct uses of high and low rotary frequencies ( Barbero et al., 2025 ) . These observations are relevant to SFA because it averages keys after positional encoding, so its coarse blocks aggregate both content and positional phase. The resulting connection between spatial averaging and frequency response is analyzed in Appendix A.9 .

SFA establishes scale-free structure as an effective design principle for efficient, high-quality diffusion transformers. 1 Introduction Generating coherent visual content at high resolution requires models that capture both fine detail and long-range structure. Diffusion transformers (DiTs) have achieved strong image-generation performance by combining scalable transformer backbones with iterative denoising ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) . However, the quadratic cost of all-to-all attention becomes a major constraint as spatial resolution grows, particularly for direct pixel-space generation with PixelFlow ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . Substantially reducing this cost while matching or exceeding the generation quality of full attention remains an open problem. Existing approaches address different parts of this challenge. FlashAttention improves exact attention through memory-efficient tiling and parallel execution ( Dao et al., 2022 ; Dao, 2024 ) . Its arithmetic cost remains quadratic in token count. Linear attention uses feature-map aggregation to reduce this cost to linear complexity ( Katharopoulos et al., 2020 ; Choromanski et al., 2021 ) . However, the finite feature representations underlying this efficiency trade computational cost against approximation fidelity, making preservation of pretrained softmax interactions a separate challenge. Sparse methods such as Log-linear Sparse Attention (LLSA) ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) reduce interactions through hierarchical selection. Selection adds runtime overhead and omits fine interactions outside the selected regions, which can limit generation quality. Hierarchical attention offers structured global approximations, with H-Transformer-1D ( Zhu & Soricut, 2021 ) developed for one-dimensional sequences. Fast Multipole Attention (FMA) ( Kang et al., 2025 ) extends multilevel computation to image classification tasks using learned pooling and separate softmax at each scale, which complicates efficient kernel implementation and precludes direct resolution extrapolation and drop-in fine-tuning from full-attention checkpoints. These limitations restrict its applicability to long sequences and large pretrained generative models. The remaining challenge is to combine subquadratic cost, efficient execution, and generation quality competitive with full attention in both training from scratch and adaptation. Scale-free laws, widely studied in statistical physics, appear in natural images as approximate scale invariance and power spectra close to an inverse-square law ( Field, 1987 ; Ruderman & Bialek, 1994 ) . Consistent with this spatial prior, we observe an approximate power law in the aggregate radial attention of pretrained PixelFlow, whereas random initialization gives a nearly flat profile (Figure 1 (C)). Motivated by this observation, we introduce Scale-Free Attention (SFA) , which preserves exact local interactions and partitions the remaining image into progressively larger blocks, each represented by its mean key and value. SFA adds the logarithm of each block’s token count to its logit and applies a single softmax to all local tokens and block summaries. Our contributions are threefold. Scale-free attention. By combining mean pooling, a log ⁡ | B | \log|B| correction for spatial blocks B B containing | B | |B| tokens, and a shared softmax over a two-dimensional scale-free hierarchy, SFA retains the original attention projections without additional parameters or hyperparameters. For N N tokens, both forward and backward passes have O ⁡ ( N ​ log ⁡ N ) O(N\log N) complexity. In our experiments, SFA achieves higher generation quality than the three efficient-attention baselines and matches or exceeds the performance of full attention (Figure 2 (C,D)). Fast Triton kernels. We implement SFA in Triton ( Tillet et al., 2019 ) , using recursive pooling and kernels that fuse attention across spatial scales. Figures 4 and 5 in Appendix B illustrate the forward and backward kernel architectures, respectively. At 262,144 tokens, SFA achieves 357.3 × 357.3\times forward and 265.6 × 265.6\times backward speedups over FlashAttention on an RTX 5090 (Figure 2 (A,B)). Approximation guarantees. For a fixed spatial partition, we prove that SFA uniquely minimizes reverse Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence to full attention among blockwise uniform distributions, and bound attention-mass and output errors under logarithmic spatial logits. 2 Related Work Generative modeling. Appendix C.8 gives the four variant definitions, detailed quality results, and efficiency analysis. 6 Discussion and Limitations The spatial hierarchy in SFA suggests a natural extension to video generation through spatiotemporal partitioning. Such a hierarchy could preserve fine interactions within nearby frames while summarizing increasingly distant regions across both space and time. Mean pooling, token-count correction, and shared normalization apply to these spatiotemporal blocks, with motion and the different rates of spatial and temporal variation guiding their shapes and resolutions. Adapting temporal coarsening to these correlations throughout denoising would be a promising direction for balancing generation quality and computational cost. Beyond video generation, this principle could support action-conditioned visual world models, which predict how an environment evolves in response to actions ( Bruce et al., 2024 ) . A hierarchy over past observations could retain detailed interactions with recent frames and conditioning actions while representing older visual context through coarser summaries, potentially making longer histories more affordable during prediction. In a causal formulation, each pooled summary and its token count would need to include only the history visible to its query. The resulting partition would thus need to respect both spatiotemporal structure and causal ordering. Our study focuses on regular two-dimensional image grids, leaving irregular grids unexplored. Additionally, further acceleration is constrained by the remaining transformer components: our FFHQ experiments show that the computational bottleneck has shifted from attention to projections, feed-forward networks, and other operations. Optimizing the transformer block as a whole therefore remains a direction for future work. 7 Conclusion By combining a scale-free spatial partition with mean aggregation, token-count correction, and a single softmax across scales, SFA gives an O ⁡ ( N ​ log ⁡ N ) O(N\log N) attention mechanism with a precise approximation relationship to full attention and a spatial inductive bias suited to image generation. Our analysis links approximation quality to within-block logit variation and explains why relative spatial resolution is appropriate for power-law interactions. Empirically, SFA achieves the best quality in the five-method PixelFlow comparison at 40 epochs, improves FFHQ generation, and preserves full-attention quality under matched fine-tuning budgets in PixelFlow and Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium. Together with substantial attention and whole-model speedups, these results support its use in both training new generators and adapting pretrained ones.
